IV. Discussion

RBCC proteins are crucial to normal cellular functions. The normal as well as disrupted function, which may contribute to neoplasia, of CAR-1 can be better understood with the characterization of the role of particular protein domains in localization and complex formation.

With the immunocytochemistry results in consideration, we can begin to reason whether the complex formation is unique or linked with other characterized RING finger and RBCC family proteins such as BRCA-1 or PML. Further study with coimmunoprecipitation experiments could identify specific binding partners of CAR-1 found in macromolecular structures.

Results from the immunohistochemistry, showing a concentration of CAR-1 staining around ductal structures, are particularly significant because the majority of breast cancers primarily originate in ductal epithelial cells. These data suggest that mutations disrupt the normal function of CAR-1 protein in these ductal regions, suggesting the role of CAR-1 in tumorigenesis.
Further studies involving CAR-1 gene transfection and targeted gene knockouts in mice will hopefully provide more evidence to determine if CAR-1 is a tumor suppressor gene.

In light of theories such as the “two-hit” model of tumorigenesis that proposes that tumor suppressor genes generate a tumorigenic effect when both alleles become inactivated by mutation or chromosomal deletion, it is of supreme importance to isolate tumor suppressor genes.³ By pinpointing possible causation of tumorigenesis, further investigation into the development and progression of human cancer can be performed, and, optimistically, mechanisms of cancer will be understood to engender a better understanding of cancer.
